# Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations

Chaipat Tirapongprasert Affiliation: Columbia University
Email: [t.chaipat@columbia.edu](mailto:)    Matthew Ho
Affiliation: Institute for Advanced Study

###### Abstract

Calibrating a cosmological simulation is an expensive, high-dimensional
parameter optimization task. Previous works employ Bayesian optimization
for automation, which treats the simulator as a black box and precludes
the incorporation of human domain knowledge or workflow into the
selection policy. We propose AgenticTuner , an agentic calibration
pipeline with a present-day large language model serving as the
optimizer who proposes the next parameter trial. We show that these
agents can achieve competitive calibration performance at a fraction of
the CPU cost when they are given informal, human-readable priors (such
as codebase, documentation, and heuristic guides that seasoned
scientists may possess). We hope this work serves as an early step
toward AI scientists that can carry out complex, long-horizon scientific
tasks. A starter code is available on GitHub.¹¹ 1
[https://github.com/chaipattira/SimulationCalibrator](https://github.com/chaipattira/SimulationCalibrator)

## 1 Introduction

Cosmological hydrodynamic simulations necessitate a set of physical
parameters that regulate processes like stellar and active galactic
nuclei (AGN) feedback. These parameters cannot be determined from first
principles and must be adjusted for the simulation to reproduce known
observables. To produce simulations and emulators that generalize across
plausible physics, large simulation suites, such as CAMELS
\[[25](#bib.bib24)\] and DREAMS \[[22](#bib.bib25)\], vary parameters
over wide ranges. The problem is that many of these parameters,
particularly those governing astrophysical feedback, lack strong
physical priors, making it unclear how to center the sampled ranges
around values that are consistent with actual observations.

To produce a well-calibrated simulation, practitioners can either
manually iterate through a trial-and-error tuning procedure based on
prior knowledge and experience or automate the search with Bayesian
optimization \[[20](#bib.bib11), [1](#bib.bib7), [21](#bib.bib3),
[13](#bib.bib29), BO;\]. Despite its effectiveness, BO cannot easily
absorb the vast corpus of domain knowledge already present in natural
language such as scientific papers or simulation code. Customized
kernels and surrogates  \[[9](#bib.bib21), [10](#bib.bib20)\] can be
used to encode structural assumptions from documentation and previous
experimental logs, but these methods are challenging to formalize and
implement. Recent research  \[[29](#bib.bib4), [16](#bib.bib6),
[17](#bib.bib5)\] proposed replacing the acquisition function with large
language models (LLMs), prompting them to propose the next query point
conditioned on a textual description of the problem and search space.
However, such direct prompting is inadequate for rich, long-horizon
tasks, such as ours, which require a large amount of relevant context
that cannot be accommodated in a single context window.

In this paper, we present AgenticTuner , an agentic simulation
calibration pipeline in which an LLM agent can reason about the search
landscape, form hypotheses, and retrieve the relevant domain knowledge
priors. Like a human scientist, it can (a) consult documentation, source
code, or a running record of previous experiments and (b) query
low-resolution proxy simulation to narrow down a portion of the
parameter space before committing to an expensive run. Our findings show
that AgenticTuner can match the calibration performance of a Bayesian
optimization baseline at a fraction of the simulation cost,
demonstrating the practical value of encoding domain priors into the
selection policy. The agents can also adjust their strategies based on
budget and evaluation history.

## 2 Problem and Experimental Setup

#### Task.

We approach the calibration of an expensive, intractable-likelihood
simulator \[[12](#bib.bib1), [19](#bib.bib2), [21](#bib.bib3)\] as an
optimization problem. For a chosen parameter vector
$`\theta_{\rm true}\in\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}`$, we run a forward
simulator $`\mathcal{M}`$ to generate a target observable
$`x^{\rm target}=\mathcal{M}(\theta_{\rm true})`$. The goal of
calibration is to search for a point estimate

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\hat{\theta}\;=\;\argmin_{\theta\,\in\,\Theta}\;d\big(\mathcal{M}(\theta),\,x^{\rm target}\big)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\textstyle\sum_{t}c(\theta_{t})\,\leq\,B\,,
``` |  | (1) |

where $`d(\cdot,\cdot)`$ is a discrepancy metric defined via the
statistical goodness-of-fit of the observable and $`c(\theta)`$ is the
computational cost of running one forward pass of the simulator. As a
constraint, we specify that the total cost of running these trials
(e.g., CPU hours, wall-clock time) cannot exceed a predetermined budget
$`B`$. For cosmological simulators, $`\mathcal{M}`$ is typically a very
complex non-linear mapping, making Eq.
[1](#S2.E1 "In Task. ‣ 2 Problem and Experimental Setup ‣ Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations")
a non-convex optimization objective.

![Refer to caption](2610.40685v1/Untitled_presentation_cropped.png)

Figure 1: Overview of AgenticTuner. At each step $`t`$, the agent can
observe the workspace $`o_{t,i}`$ or run a low-resolution probe before
submitting $`\theta_{t+1}`$ to the simulator $`\mathcal{M}`$. If the
trial converges, the loop terminates; otherwise, the agent’s context is
cleared, and the loop restarts with the updated $`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$.

#### Baseline.

A standard non-convex optimization technique is BO \[[20](#bib.bib11),
[1](#bib.bib7)\], which treats
Eq. [1](#S2.E1 "In Task. ‣ 2 Problem and Experimental Setup ‣ Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations")
as a sequential decision process. At each step $`t`$, BO fits a
probabilistic surrogate model to the trial history
$`\mathcal{D}_{t}=\{(\theta_{\tau},d_{\tau},c_{\tau})\}_{\tau\leq t}`$,
and uses an acquisition function $`\alpha(\theta;\mathcal{D}_{t})`$ to
propose the next point,
$`\theta_{t+1}=\arg\max_{\theta\in\Theta}\;\alpha(\theta;\mathcal{D}_{t})`$.
The most common surrogate is a Gaussian process \[[20](#bib.bib11),
GP;\], with tree-based and density-based alternatives also in use (e.g.,
TPE \[[5](#bib.bib22)\], SMAC \[[15](#bib.bib23)\]). Regardless of
surrogate choice, BO treats the optimization process as a black box with
a non-informative prior, which prevents the integration of
domain-specific knowledge or workflow into the selection policy. We
choose GP as the baseline because it was the most sample-efficient
method in preliminary experiments comparing multiple derivative-free
optimizers for this class of problem.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Simulation and Discrepancy Metric Details ‣ Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations")
outlines our baseline implementation of GP-BO.

#### Configuration.

We center our study on a sufficiently challenging numerical task of
calibrating a cosmological simulation. We use MP-Gadget
\[[6](#bib.bib9), [18](#bib.bib10)\], a particle-based (N-body)
cosmological simulation that evolves dark matter, gas, stars, and black
holes via gravity and hydrodynamics, as the forward simulator
$`\mathcal{M}`$. For a chosen 12-parameter vector $`\theta_{\rm true}`$
(defined in
Table [1](#A2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ B.3 Parameter space ‣ Appendix B Task Description Prompts ‣ Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations")),
$`\mathcal{M}`$ generates the target observable $`x^{\rm target}`$ from
Eq. [1](#S2.E1 "In Task. ‣ 2 Problem and Experimental Setup ‣ Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations")
in the form of a matter power spectrum
$`P^{\rm target}(k;\theta_{\rm true})\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\rm bins}}`$: a
statistic measuring matter clustering strength as a function of scale
$`k`$, evaluated at $`n_{\rm bins}`$ Fourier bins. For a given
simulation configuration, this vector is expected to have intrinsic
noise distributed as an i.i.d. isotropic Gaussian.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Simulation and Discrepancy Metric Details ‣ Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations")
provides more details on simulation and job settings.

We instantiate the discrepancy $`d(\cdot,\cdot)`$ from
Eq. [1](#S2.E1 "In Task. ‣ 2 Problem and Experimental Setup ‣ Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations")
as the mode-weighted reduced chi-squared between simulated and target
spectra,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\tilde{\chi}^{2}=\frac{\chi^{2}}{n_{\rm bins}},\qquad\text{where}\qquad\chi^{2}=\sum_{i}\frac{\big(P_{i}^{\rm sim}-P_{i}^{\rm target}\big)^{2}}{\sigma_{i}^{2}},
``` |  | (2) |

and $`\sigma_{i}^{2}`$ is the cosmic variance, i.e. the statistical
noise from measuring clustering in a finite volume (full expression and
$`k`$-range in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Simulation and Discrepancy Metric Details ‣ Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations")).
A trial is considered converged when $`\tilde{\chi}^{2}<1`$, i.e., once
the simulated spectrum matches the target to within the cosmic-variance
noise floor. The CPU hours spent on trial $`t`$ determine its cost
$`c(\theta_{t})`$ from
Eq. [1](#S2.E1 "In Task. ‣ 2 Problem and Experimental Setup ‣ Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations").

## 3 Methods

#### Loop design.

AgenticTuner is an agentic simulation calibration system that replaces
an acquisition function with an LLM as the optimizer (see
Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Task. ‣ 2 Problem and Experimental Setup ‣ Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations")).
The central loop of AgenticTuner is orchestrated by the external
harness, which is separate from and independent of the LLM. Each
iteration $`t`$ begins with the instantiation of a stateless LLM
instance within a sandboxed container that conceals the hidden ground
truth $`\theta_{\rm true}`$. Because LLM performance has been shown to
deteriorate with a monotonically increasing context
window \[[8](#bib.bib12), [27](#bib.bib13), [26](#bib.bib14)\], we opt
to clear the context \[[3](#bib.bib19)\] after the LLM calls an
expensive simulator for the proposed trial $`\theta_{t+1}`$. When the
simulation is finished, the harness mediates the evaluation process by
calculating $`\tilde{\chi}^{2}(\theta_{t+1})`$ and either restarting the
loop with a fresh agent or stopping the search if $`\tilde{\chi}^{2}<1`$
or a fixed CPU-hour budget is exhausted.

Figure 2: Reduced-$`\tilde{\chi}^{2}`$ vs. trial number for
AgenticTuner (teal) and BO baseline (orange). We present ten
representative runs from our 20 experiments for legibility. To stress
test our algorithm, we reduced the allowed CPU budget for both methods
in the bottom row, which explains the total lack of convergence in BO
runs.

#### Exploration.

Let $`t`$ index expensive evaluations and $`i`$ index computationally
free actions taken by the LLM agent in between evaluations. Submitting
$`\theta_{t+1}`$ to the simulator $`\mathcal{M}`$ is the only action
that incurs cost $`c(\theta_{t+1})`$. Before doing so, the agent may
choose to perform a number of cost-free observations $`o_{t,i}`$ and/or
append to the workspace,
$`\left\{\mathcal{P},\ \mathcal{C},\,P^{\rm target},\,\mathcal{G},\,\mathcal{D}_{t},\ \mathcal{N}_{t}^{(i)}\right\},`$
which functions as the working memory of the recently spawned agent. The
problem file $`\mathcal{P}`$ (see
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Task Description Prompts ‣ Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations"))
first orients the LLM by providing a natural-language description of the
task, constraints, and a list of tunable parameters (and their allowed
bounds). The LLM also has read-only access to the forward simulator’s
codebase $`\mathcal{C}`$ for further investigation. Given the LLM’s
versatile ability to reason in natural language and adapt its strategies
through in-context learning \[[7](#bib.bib16)\], we expect it to match a
human scientist’s search performance when given the same domain
knowledge about the problem and search space. This motivates the guide
$`\mathcal{G}`$ (see
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Guide and documentation ‣ Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations")),
which contains code documentation and distilled, ‘trial-and-error’
intuitions human scientists rely on when fine-tuning simulations under a
constrained budget \[[28](#bib.bib18)\]. The agent may use the informal
prior encoded in the guide to decide which regions of the parameter
space to explore or exploit. The trial history $`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$ and
the lab notebook $`\mathcal{N}_{t}^{(i)}`$ are append-only.
$`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$ is the accumulated log of past evaluations
(parameter vector with simulated spectra), while
$`\mathcal{N}_{t}^{(i)}`$ is the agent’s commentary (e.g., reasoning,
hypotheses, and lessons learned) written for future agent invocations.
To avoid repeating previous failed attempts, the current agent may
consult these records before making a decision.

#### Low-resolution probe.

Aside from inspecting the workspace, the agent can invoke a cheap,
low-fidelity matter power spectrum simulator
$`\textsc{Probe}(\theta_{\rm cosmo})`$, implemented using
CAMB \[[14](#bib.bib15)\], to obtain a dark-matter-only proxy for the
power spectrum. The resulting power spectrum is an approximation in that
Probe only accepts cosmological parameters and thus neglects the effects
of the remaining baryonic or subgrid parameters. We expect the agent to
use the low-resolution proxy to narrow down the relevant cosmology
before proceeding with the expensive high-resolution simulation.

Figure 3: Per-invocation timeline of AgenticTuner ’s reasoning and tool
calls, early vs. late in the run (pooled over independent runs; five
shown per panel to save space). Actions are fetched and classified from
the saved traces; *Other* covers miscellaneous sanity-check code. Legend
percentages (early/late) give each action’s total share across all runs.

## 4 Experiments and Results

To compare AgenticTuner and BO baseline in reaching convergence within a
fixed budget, we run the experiment 20 times with different random
seeds, true parameters, and simulator initial conditions.

#### Calibration performance.

Our results show that by incorporating the informal prior into the
selection policy, AgenticTuner achieves convergence using a median of
8.5 simulation calls (68% CI: 6.0–14.1). In comparison, the simulation
cost is nearly twice as low as BO, which requires a median of 17.5 calls
(14.4–24.2).
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Loop design. ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations")
depicts the reduced $`\tilde{\chi}^{2}`$ trajectory for some example
runs. We find that the trajectory of AgenticTuner (teal) shows a
consistent downward trend with occasional bumps, while the BO baseline
(orange) fluctuates for many trials before occasionally dropping.
Because BO’s oscillatory trajectory persists well beyond the early
exploration phase, we hypothesize that the LLM agent’s advantage is due
in part to its access to informative physical priors.

#### Anatomy of reasoning.

To gain insight into the LLM’s decision-making process while tackling a
long-horizon task, we examine the lab notebook and reasoning trace
during the first and last half of each run’s invocations (see
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Low-resolution probe. ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations")).
The LLM begins each new invocation with no memory other than what is
written to disk, necessitating a fixed reorientation cost (about 30% of
the budget) by scanning the workspace files. During the early stages,
the agent focuses on calling cheap Probe proxies (7%) and doing residual
analysis (6%), initially to localize the cosmological parameters and
later to narrow the sweep of each. It also checks for degeneracies
between the parameters before submitting the expensive trial. After
pinning the cosmological parameters, the agent stops relying on Probe in
later reasoning, as expected, and switches its token use to curate
findings in the notebook $`\mathcal{N}_{t}^{(i)}`$ and analyze the
accumulating trial history $`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$ (26%). This shift in
reasoning demonstrates that the LLM uses a hierarchical strategy that
evolves based on past history and remaining budget.

Figure 4: Per-trial parameter-recovery error
$`|\theta-\theta_{\rm fid}|/({\rm hi}-{\rm lo})`$ across two
representative converged AgenticTuner runs; colored curves are the
parameters the agent chose to tune.

#### Parameter recovery.

Across all runs, AgenticTuner largely changes 2-5 parameters from their
starting values, leaving the remaining parameters at the default values.
This selective choice implies that the power spectra are constrained by
a small set of parameters and that tuning all twelve parameters is not
necessary to achieve convergence.
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Anatomy of reasoning. ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations")
shows the error in each parameter for two representative converged runs.
Due to degeneracies in power spectra, different points in parameter
space can map to the same observables \[[23](#bib.bib27)\], which means
that some parameters of the converged run may be further away from the
ground truth than they started. In Panel A, the agent chooses to tune
the wind feedback, whereas in Panel B, the agent achieves convergence by
tuning $`\sigma_{8}`$ early. We note that the observed divergences in
parameter space due to degeneracies are not a limitation of
AgenticTuner , but rather a true physical degeneracy for this class of
observable \[[24](#bib.bib26), [2](#bib.bib28)\]. Our guide (see
Box [C](#A3 "Appendix C Guide and documentation ‣ Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations")
in the Appendix) includes some of the well-known degeneracies and
proposes corresponding recommendations, such as fixing $`\Omega_{m}`$
and using $`\sigma_{8}`$ as the main cosmology handle.

## 5 Conclusion

In this work, we present AgenticTuner , an agentic calibration system
that uses an LLM agent to propose the parameter point based on trial
history and human-authored priors. We evaluate our system in calibrating
a costly cosmological simulation and find that AgenticTuner outperforms
the Bayesian optimization baseline in simulation cost across all runs.
Auditing the reasoning trace of the LLM agent demonstrates its ability
to adapt the search strategy during a run from active tool use to
synthesizing previous findings. These results suggest that
natural-language priors significantly improve the selection process.

Future work includes evaluating AgenticTuner on a broader set of
observables and ablating its context components (guide, codebase,
low-resolution probe) to isolate what drives sample efficiency. It would
also be useful to replicate our findings with open-weight LLMs, which we
anticipate will achieve comparable calibration performance. Finally, we
plan to let the agent configure simulation volume and resolution for
dynamic cost allocation and to benchmark its search strategy against a
human scientist.

## Appendix A Simulation and Discrepancy Metric Details

#### Simulation settings.

We use $`N_{\rm grid}=128`$ (i.e., $`128^{3}`$ particles) and
$`L_{\rm box}=100`$ Mpc/h, matching the target box specified in the task
prompt
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Task Description Prompts ‣ Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations"));
box size sets the simulated volume and largest resolvable scale, grid
resolution sets the smallest resolvable scale. All runs were submitted
as Slurm jobs \[[11](#bib.bib8)\], each with 32 CPU cores.

#### Discrepancy metric.

$`\sigma_{i}^{2}=2(P_{i}^{\rm target})^{2}/N_{i}`$ is the cosmic
variance of a power spectrum estimator averaged over $`N_{i}`$
independent Fourier modes. We drop bins below the fundamental mode
$`k_{\min}=2\pi/L_{\rm box}`$ and above the grid’s Nyquist frequency
$`k_{\max}=\pi\,N_{\rm grid}/L_{\rm box}`$.

#### BO baseline configuration.

Our BO baseline employs Optuna’s GPSampler \[[1](#bib.bib7)\] to
minimize $`\chi^{2}`$ across the 12-dimensional box $`\Theta`$. The
optimization process begins with five rounds of random exploration,
after which the GP surrogate handles the selection. Failed trials
receive a large finite penalty ($`\chi^{2}=10^{7}`$) instead of being
pruned, ensuring the surrogate remains well-defined when trials are
scarce. On each restart, the full trial history $`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$ is
replayed into a new study rather than resumed incrementally. The search
ends when $`\tilde{\chi}^{2}<1`$ or the CPU-hour budget is exhausted.

## Appendix B Task Description Prompts

We have included the full user prompt below for reproducibility
purposes. All LLM calls use Claude Sonnet 5 \[[4](#bib.bib17)\]. A
single calibration run fits within the monthly usage allowance of a
\$$`20`$ Claude Pro plan, making the approach accessible without metered
API billing.

### B.1 Problem Statement

Each trial is executed by a new agent instance with no conversational
memory. It maintains continuity by reading and writing files
(lab_notebook.md, trial_state.yaml). The first section of the prompt
introduces the agent to the task and the workspace.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### B.2 Low-fidelity CAMB pre-screening

In our setup, full MP-Gadget trials cost CPU hours, while a
halofit-based nonlinear power spectrum is considered free. Before
allocating funds for the actual run, the agent is encouraged to narrow
the five cosmological parameters at a low cost by exposing this as an
explicit, unmetered tool.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### B.3 Parameter space

| Parameter | Role | Prior box |
|----|----|----|
| $`\Omega_{m}`$ (Omega0) | cosmological | $`[0.20,0.45]`$ |
| $`\Omega_{b}`$ (OmegaBaryon) | cosmological | $`[0.03,0.06]`$ |
| $`\sigma_{8}`$ (Sigma8) | cosmological | $`[0.60,1.00]`$ |
| $`n_{s}`$ (PrimordialIndex) | cosmological | $`[0.90,1.05]`$ |
| $`h`$ (HubbleParam) | cosmological | $`[0.60,0.80]`$ |
| WindSigma0 | wind mass-loading | $`[200,500]`$ km/s |
| WindSpeedFactor | wind kick speed | $`[1.5,6.0]`$ |
| WindFreeTravelLength | wind decoupling | $`[5,60]`$ |
| WindFreeTravelDensFac | wind decoupling | $`[0.02,0.5]`$ |
| BlackHoleFeedbackFactor | AGN feedback | $`[0.01,0.15]`$ |
| BlackHoleAccretionFactor | AGN accretion | $`[20,300]`$ |
| SeedBlackHoleMass | AGN seeding | $`[5\times 10^{-6},10^{-4}]`$ |

Table 1: The twelve-parameter search box $`\Theta`$.

This section provides a list of tunable parameters, including five
cosmological parameters that a linear/halofit calculation can reasonably
constrain and the remainder seven subgrid feedback parameters.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### B.4 Trial execution protocol

Because the agent is to submit a multi-hour Slurm job on a shared node,
we provide boilerplate code that handles the minutia of such
orchestration.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### B.5 Recording results and convergence criteria

To avoid post-hoc rationalization, the agent must write their predicted
reasoning before seeing the trial outcome. The two hard stopping
conditions are a reduced-$`\chi^{2}<1`$ convergence criterion and the
CPU-hour budget cap.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### B.6 Boundaries against finding the answer key

An unconstrained agent could bypass the need to infer the ground-truth
parameters from simulation output and instead search for them directly
on the filesystem. This section closes the loophole procedurally by
instructing the agent not to waste extra tokens trying to look for the
answer. Our harness also enforces the constraint structurally by
excluding the judge/ directory from the session’s sandbox view.
````
